explanation: China has no hygiene-based taboo on the left hand like South Asia or the Middle East. Chopsticks were traditionally held in the right hand mainly to avoid elbows and sticks colliding with neighbors at a shared table, not because the left hand was considered unclean, and left-handed chopstick use is increasingly common and accepted today.
local_tip: Use whichever hand feels natural for your chopsticks; if you're left-handed, just be mindful of your elbow room at a crowded table.
regional_note: In Xinjiang and other Muslim-majority areas of China, broader Islamic custom can make the left hand less preferred for eating, similar to Muslim practice elsewhere.

also_check.note: The left hand is reserved for bathroom hygiene, so eating or passing food with it is considered unclean.
The left hand is reserved for unclean tasks; eating or passing food with it is considered offensive.
There's no stigma on the left hand; chopstick etiquette instead focuses on rules like not pointing or stabbing food with chopsticks.
